title: CUET Physics Test 9
subject: Physics (Code: 322)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Physics - 322.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Physics papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format and level (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Physics, Class XII, Parts I and II (rationalised edition)
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
Calculators are not allowed; numbers are chosen so the working can be done by hand.

questions.sub_topic: Refraction and dispersion — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Light bends towards the normal on entering an optically denser medium.
(B) The frequency of light does not change on refraction.
(C) In glass, red light travels more slowly than violet light.
(D) A prism deviates violet light more than red light.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: glass has a smaller index for red, so red travels faster than violet.
Why not the others: (A) it slows down and bends towards the normal. (B) frequency is fixed by the source. (D) violet has the larger index. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Larger index means slower light and more bending.

questions.sub_topic: Capacitance of an isolated metal sphere of radius 9 cm
questions.question: The capacitance of an isolated metal sphere of radius 9 cm in air is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10 pF
Given: \(R = 0.09\) m
Formula: \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0R = \dfrac{R}{9 \times 10^9}\)
Step 1: \(C = \dfrac{0.09}{9 \times 10^9} = 1 \times 10^{-11}\) F
Step 2: \(C = 10\) pF
Common mistake: 100 pF (D) takes 9 cm as 0.9 m.
Key point: Even a large sphere has a tiny capacitance; the farad is a huge unit.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Wavelength that gives a stopping potential of 2 V on a 2.13 eV metal
questions.question: A metal has a work function of 2.13 eV. The wavelength of light that gives a stopping potential of 2 V is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 300 nm
Given: \(\phi_0 = 2.13\) eV, \(V_0 = 2\) V
Formula: \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \phi_0 + eV_0\)
Step 1: Photon energy \(= 2.13 + 2 = 4.13\) eV
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{4.13} \approx 300\) nm
Common mistake: 582 nm (C) uses the work function alone, which gives the threshold. 620 nm (A) uses only the 2 eV.
Key point: The photon pays the work function first; the rest is kinetic energy.

questions.sub_topic: Groupings of 4 Ω resistors in increasing order of resistance
questions.question:
Using identical \(4\ \Omega\) resistors, arrange these groupings in increasing order of equivalent resistance:
(A) two in series
(B) two in parallel
(C) three in parallel
(D) one in series with a parallel pair
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Step 1: (A) \(4 + 4 = 8\ \Omega\); (B) \(\dfrac{4}{2} = 2\ \Omega\)
Step 2: (C) \(\dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\ \Omega\); (D) \(4 + 2 = 6\ \Omega\)
Step 3: Increasing: (C), (B), (D), (A)
Common mistake: Placing (B) below (C); more resistors in parallel give less resistance.
Key point: \(n\) equal resistors in parallel give \(\dfrac{R}{n}\).

questions.sub_topic: Scientists and their work on electromagnetic waves
questions.question:
Match each scientist in List-I with the work in List-II.

List-I
(A) Maxwell
(B) Hertz
(C) J. C. Bose
(D) Marconi

List-II
(I) First produced and detected EM waves in the laboratory
(II) Sent EM waves over many kilometres
(III) Predicted EM waves from theory
(IV) Produced waves of wavelength 5 mm to 25 mm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Maxwell's equations predicted the waves (III)
Step 2: Hertz produced and detected them in 1887 (I)
Step 3: Bose worked with millimetre waves (IV)
Step 4: Marconi transmitted them over long distances (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); Maxwell predicted, Hertz demonstrated.
Key point: Theory came first; experiment confirmed it about twenty years later.

questions.sub_topic: Resistivity and temperature — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The resistivity of a metal increases with temperature.
(B) The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as its temperature rises.
(C) Manganin has a very small temperature coefficient, so it is used for standard resistors.
(D) The resistivity of a wire doubles when its length is doubled.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) more frequent collisions shorten the relaxation time. (B) more carriers are freed across the band gap. (C) its resistance hardly changes when it warms.
Why not the others: (D) is false: resistivity is a property of the material; doubling the length doubles the resistance, not the resistivity. Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Resistance depends on shape; resistivity does not.

questions.sub_topic: Conditions for total internal reflection
questions.question: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels:
options: A) from air into glass at any angle
B) from glass into air below the critical angle
C) from glass into air beyond the critical angle
D) from water into glass beyond the critical angle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) from glass into air beyond the critical angle
Why: Light must go from a denser to a rarer medium, at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) go from rarer to denser, where it cannot happen. (B) below the critical angle the light refracts out.
Key point: Denser to rarer, and beyond the critical angle.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Accelerating voltage for an electron wavelength of 0.1227 nm
questions.question: Through what potential difference must an electron be accelerated from rest to have a de Broglie wavelength of 0.1227 nm?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 100 V
Given: \(\lambda = 0.1227\) nm
Formula: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\) nm
Step 1: \(\sqrt{V} = \dfrac{1.227}{0.1227} = 10\)
Step 2: \(V = 100\) V
Common mistake: 10 V (A) forgets to square.
Key point: Halving the wavelength needs four times the voltage.

questions.sub_topic: Four hydrogen jumps ranked by the energy they release
questions.question:
Arrange these hydrogen transitions in increasing order of the energy of the emitted photon:
(A) \(n = 4 \to n = 3\)
(B) \(n = 3 \to n = 2\)
(C) \(n = 2 \to n = 1\)
(D) \(n = 4 \to n = 2\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B), (D), (C)
Step 1: \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\): \(E_1 = -13.6\), \(E_2 = -3.4\), \(E_3 = -1.51\), \(E_4 = -0.85\) eV
Step 2: (A) 0.66 eV; (B) 1.89 eV; (D) 2.55 eV; (C) 10.2 eV
Step 3: Increasing: (A), (B), (D), (C)
Common mistake: (C) ranks by the upper level alone; \(4 \to 2\) crosses a larger gap than \(3 \to 2\).
Key point: Levels crowd together as \(n\) grows, so high-\(n\) jumps release little energy.

questions.sub_topic: Kinetic energy of an α-particle accelerated through 1 kV
questions.question: An α-particle starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. Its kinetic energy is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3.2 \times 10^{-16}\) J
Given: \(q = 2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(V = 1000\) V
Formula: \(K = qV\)
Step 1: \(K = 2e \times 1000\ \text{V} = 2\) keV
Step 2: \(K = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \times 1000 = 3.2 \times 10^{-16}\) J
Common mistake: \(1.6 \times 10^{-16}\) J (A) uses the charge \(e\). \(2 \times 10^3\) J (B) is 2000 eV written as joules.
Key point: An α-particle gains \(2\) eV per volt.

questions.sub_topic: Average power in an RL circuit with R = 60 Ω and X_L = 80 Ω
questions.question: A \(60\ \Omega\) resistor and an inductor of reactance \(80\ \Omega\) are in series across a 200 V (rms) supply. The average power drawn is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 240 W
Given: \(R = 60\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 80\ \Omega\), \(V = 200\) V
Formula: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}\), \(P = I^2R\)
Step 1: \(Z = 100\ \Omega\), so \(I = 2\) A
Step 2: \(P = 4 \times 60 = 240\) W (power factor \(\dfrac{60}{100} = 0.6\))
Common mistake: 400 W (A) is \(VI\), which ignores the power factor. 320 W (C) uses \(X_L\) in place of \(R\).
Key point: Only the resistor uses power; an ideal inductor uses none.

questions.sub_topic: Deviation of a symmetric ray through a crown-glass prism
questions.question: A ray passes symmetrically through a \(60^\circ\) glass prism of index 1.5. The deviation it suffers is about (\(\sin 48.6^\circ = 0.75\)):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(37.2^\circ\)
Given: \(A = 60^\circ\), \(n = 1.5\)
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + D_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\dfrac{A + D_m}{2} = 1.5 \times \sin 30^\circ = 0.75\), so \(\dfrac{A + D_m}{2} = 48.6^\circ\)
Step 2: \(D_m = 97.2^\circ - 60^\circ = 37.2^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(30^\circ\) (A) uses the thin-prism rule \((n - 1)A\), which fails for a \(60^\circ\) prism. \(48.6^\circ\) (C) stops at the half-angle.
Key point: The thin-prism formula holds only for small angles.

questions.sub_topic: Current in a series RC circuit with R = 30 Ω and X_C = 40 Ω
questions.question: A \(30\ \Omega\) resistor and a capacitor of reactance \(40\ \Omega\) are in series across a 100 V (rms) supply. The rms current is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 A
Given: \(R = 30\ \Omega\), \(X_C = 40\ \Omega\), \(V = 100\) V
Formula: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}\), \(I = \dfrac{V}{Z}\)
Step 1: \(Z = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = 50\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{100}{50} = 2\) A
Common mistake: 1.43 A (A) adds \(R\) and \(X_C\) directly; they are \(90^\circ\) out of phase.
Key point: Resistance and reactance add as perpendicular sides of a triangle.

questions.sub_topic: Self-inductance from the flux through each turn
questions.question: A coil of 500 turns carries 2 A, and the magnetic flux through each turn is \(2 \times 10^{-5}\) Wb. The self-inductance of the coil is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) H
Given: \(N = 500\), \(\Phi = 2 \times 10^{-5}\) Wb, \(I = 2\) A
Formula: \(N\Phi = LI\)
Step 1: \(N\Phi = 500 \times 2 \times 10^{-5} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\) Wb
Step 2: \(L = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{2} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) H
Common mistake: \(1 \times 10^{-2}\) H (C) forgets to divide by the current. \(1 \times 10^{-5}\) H (A) ignores the 500 turns.
Key point: Inductance is the total flux linkage per unit current.

questions.sub_topic: Emf and internal resistance of two identical cells grouped
questions.question:
Two identical cells, each of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\), are grouped. Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I
(A) Emf of the series pair
(B) Emf of the parallel pair
(C) Internal resistance of the series pair
(D) Internal resistance of the parallel pair

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{r}{2}\)
(II) \(\varepsilon\)
(III) \(2r\)
(IV) \(2\varepsilon\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Step 1: In series the emfs add: \(2\varepsilon\) (IV)
Step 2: Identical cells in parallel keep the emf: \(\varepsilon\) (II)
Step 3: Series internal resistances add: \(2r\) (III)
Step 4: Two equal internal resistances in parallel: \(\dfrac{r}{2}\) (I)
Common mistake: Thinking parallel cells add their emfs; they only share the current.
Key point: Series raises voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Threshold wavelengths for four work functions
questions.question:
Match each work function in List-I with the threshold wavelength in List-II (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm).

List-I
(A) 2.0 eV
(B) 2.48 eV
(C) 3.1 eV
(D) 4.13 eV

List-II
(I) 400 nm
(II) 620 nm
(III) 300 nm
(IV) 500 nm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{1240}{\phi_0}\); (A) \(\dfrac{1240}{2} = 620\) nm (II)
Step 2: (B) \(\dfrac{1240}{2.48} = 500\) nm (IV)
Step 3: (C) \(\dfrac{1240}{3.1} = 400\) nm (I)
Step 4: (D) \(\dfrac{1240}{4.13} \approx 300\) nm (III)
Common mistake: Pairing the largest work function with the longest wavelength; they are inversely related.
Key point: A larger work function needs shorter-wavelength light.

questions.sub_topic: Ozone, microwaves and the greenhouse effect — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
(B) Radio waves have higher frequencies than microwaves.
(C) Microwave ovens heat food because water molecules absorb microwaves.
(D) Infrared radiation given out by the Earth helps keep it warm through the greenhouse effect.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A) ozone shields life from harmful UV. (C) the microwave frequency matches water's absorption. (D) greenhouse gases trap the infrared.
Why not the others: (B) is false: radio waves have longer wavelengths, and so lower frequencies, than microwaves. Options (C) and (D) include (B); (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Radio waves lie at the low-frequency end of the spectrum.

questions.sub_topic: Refractive index from the real and apparent depths of a coin
questions.question: A coin at the bottom of a liquid 12 cm deep appears, seen from above, to be 9 cm below the surface. The refractive index of the liquid is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.33
Given: real depth 12 cm, apparent depth 9 cm
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\)
Step 1: \(n = \dfrac{12}{9} = \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\)
Common mistake: 0.75 (A) inverts the ratio; an index below 1 is impossible.
Key point: Objects in a denser medium appear raised.

questions.sub_topic: Orbital speed of hydrogen's electron in the third orbit
questions.question: The speed of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is \(2.2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹. Its speed in the third orbit is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(7.3 \times 10^{5}\) m s⁻¹
Given: \(v_1 = 2.2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹, \(n = 3\)
Formula: \(v_n = \dfrac{v_1}{n}\)
Step 1: \(v_3 = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^6}{3} \approx 7.3 \times 10^5\) m s⁻¹
Common mistake: \(2.4 \times 10^5\) (B) divides by \(n^2\), the rule for energy, not speed.
Key point: Speed falls as \(\dfrac{1}{n}\), energy as \(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\).

questions.sub_topic: Four wavelengths in increasing order of frequency
questions.question:
Arrange these electromagnetic waves in increasing order of frequency:
(A) wavelength 5 cm
(B) wavelength 500 nm
(C) wavelength 1 m
(D) wavelength 0.1 nm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Step 1: \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\), so the longest wavelength has the lowest frequency
Step 2: Wavelengths: 1 m > 5 cm > 500 nm > 0.1 nm
Step 3: Increasing frequency: (C), (A), (B), (D)
Common mistake: (A) lists them in decreasing frequency.
Key point: Radio, microwave, visible and X-ray, in that order of frequency.

questions.sub_topic: Energy stored in a 2 H inductor carrying 3 A
questions.question: The energy stored in the magnetic field of a 2 H inductor carrying a steady current of 3 A is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 9 J
Given: \(L = 2\) H, \(I = 3\) A
Formula: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\)
Step 1: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 9 = 9\) J
Common mistake: 18 J (B) drops the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Key point: An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field, as a capacitor does in its electric field.

questions.sub_topic: Current in a series LCR circuit at resonance with R = 10 Ω
questions.question: A series LCR circuit with \(R = 10\ \Omega\) is connected to a 220 V (rms) supply whose frequency equals the circuit's resonant frequency. The rms current is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 22 A
Given: \(R = 10\ \Omega\), \(V = 220\) V; at resonance \(X_L = X_C\)
Formula: \(Z = R\) at resonance
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{220}{10} = 22\) A
Common mistake: 31 A (B) is the peak current, \(22\sqrt{2}\).
Key point: At resonance the reactances cancel and the current is greatest.

questions.sub_topic: Quantities for 200 sin(100πt) volts across 50 Ω
questions.question:
The voltage \(v = 200\sin(100\pi t)\) volts is applied across a \(50\ \Omega\) resistor. Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I
(A) Peak voltage
(B) rms voltage
(C) Frequency
(D) Peak current

List-II
(I) 50 Hz
(II) 4 A
(III) about 141 V
(IV) 200 V
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Step 1: The coefficient of the sine is the peak: 200 V (IV)
Step 2: \(V_{rms} = \dfrac{200}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 141\) V (III)
Step 3: \(\omega = 100\pi = 2\pi\nu\), so \(\nu = 50\) Hz (I)
Step 4: \(I_0 = \dfrac{200}{50} = 4\) A (II)
Common mistake: Reading \(100\pi\) as the frequency; it is \(\omega\), and \(\nu = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}\).
Key point: Read peak and \(\omega\) straight from \(V_0\sin\omega t\).

questions.sub_topic: Depletion layer under forward bias
questions.question: When a p–n junction is forward biased, its depletion layer:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) becomes narrower
Why: The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, pushing carriers towards the junction and shrinking the depletion layer.
Why not the others: (A) happens in reverse bias. (B) any bias changes the width. (C) it shrinks gradually; it does not vanish at every voltage.
Key point: Forward bias narrows the barrier; reverse bias widens it.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Speed of an electron on a 1 cm circle in 1 mT
questions.question: An electron moves in a circle of radius 1 cm at right angles to a magnetic field of 1 mT. Its speed is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1.76 \times 10^{6}\) m s⁻¹
Given: \(r = 0.01\) m, \(B = 10^{-3}\) T, \(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\) kg
Formula: \(r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{eBr}{m}\)
Step 1: \(eBr = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-2} = 1.6 \times 10^{-24}\)
Step 2: \(v = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-24}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 1.76 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹
Common mistake: \(9.6 \times 10^2\) (C) uses the proton's mass. (D) inverts the ratio.
Key point: The light electron circles fast in even a weak field.

questions.sub_topic: Distance of the fourth bright fringe from the centre
questions.question: In Young's experiment, \(\lambda = 500\) nm, the slits are 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1 m away. The distance of the fourth bright fringe from the central fringe is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4 mm
Given: \(\lambda = 5 \times 10^{-7}\) m, \(d = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(D = 1\) m
Formula: \(x_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)
Step 1: \(\beta = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-7} \times 1}{5 \times 10^{-4}} = 1\) mm
Step 2: \(x_4 = 4\beta = 4\) mm
Common mistake: 3.5 mm (B) is the fourth dark fringe, \(\left(n - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\beta\).
Key point: Bright fringes lie at whole multiples of the fringe width.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Force on a 2 m length of one of two parallel wires
questions.question: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry currents of 5 A and 10 A in the same direction. The force on a 2 m length of either wire is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) N, attractive
Given: \(I_1 = 5\) A, \(I_2 = 10\) A, \(d = 0.1\) m, \(L = 2\) m
Formula: \(F = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2L}{2\pi d}\)
Step 1: Per metre: \(\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 50}{0.1} = 1 \times 10^{-4}\) N m⁻¹
Step 2: On 2 m: \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) N; like currents attract
Common mistake: (A) stops at the force per metre.
Key point: Each wire feels the same force, by Newton's third law, even with unequal currents.

questions.sub_topic: Electron density in a p-type crystal from the hole density
questions.question: Pure silicon has \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{16}\) m⁻³. After doping, the hole density is \(4.5 \times 10^{22}\) m⁻³. The electron density is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5 \times 10^{9}\) m⁻³
Given: \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{16}\) m⁻³, \(n_h = 4.5 \times 10^{22}\) m⁻³
Formula: \(n_en_h = n_i^2\)
Step 1: \(n_i^2 = 2.25 \times 10^{32}\)
Step 2: \(n_e = \dfrac{2.25 \times 10^{32}}{4.5 \times 10^{22}} = 5 \times 10^9\) m⁻³
Common mistake: \(1.5 \times 10^{16}\) (C) keeps the intrinsic value; doping lowers the minority carrier density.
Key point: Raising one carrier type lowers the other, keeping \(n_en_h\) fixed.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Current in a 2 cm loop from the field at its centre
questions.question: A circular loop of radius 2 cm produces a magnetic field of \(3.14 \times 10^{-4}\) T at its centre. The current in it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10 A
Given: \(R = 0.02\) m, \(B = 3.14 \times 10^{-4}\) T
Formula: \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R} \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{2RB}{\mu_0}\)
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{2 \times 0.02 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{1.256 \times 10^{-5}}{1.256 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\) A
Common mistake: 5 A (A) uses \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{R}\), dropping the 2. 20 A (B) uses the 4 cm diameter as the radius.
Key point: The centre field of a loop is \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\), not the straight-wire \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\).

questions.sub_topic: Orbit radius and energies in hydrogen's first excited state
questions.question:
For the electron in the \(n = 2\) orbit of hydrogen, match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II (\(a_0 = 0.53\) Å).

List-I
(A) Orbit radius
(B) Total energy
(C) Kinetic energy
(D) Potential energy

List-II
(I) \(-3.4\) eV
(II) \(+3.4\) eV
(III) 2.12 Å
(IV) \(-6.8\) eV
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Step 1: \(r_n = n^2a_0 = 4 \times 0.53 = 2.12\) Å (III)
Step 2: \(E_2 = -\dfrac{13.6}{4} = -3.4\) eV (I)
Step 3: \(K = -E = +3.4\) eV (II)
Step 4: \(U = 2E = -6.8\) eV (IV)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C); the kinetic energy is positive, the total negative.
Key point: In a Bohr orbit \(K = -E\) and \(U = 2E\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Galvanometer resistance from the shunt that makes a 1 A ammeter
questions.question: A galvanometer gives full-scale deflection at 10 mA. A shunt of \(0.1\ \Omega\) turns it into an ammeter of range 1 A. The resistance of the galvanometer is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(9.9\ \Omega\)
Given: \(I_g = 0.01\) A, \(I = 1\) A, \(S = 0.1\ \Omega\)
Formula: same voltage across both: \(I_gG = (I - I_g)S\)
Step 1: \(I - I_g = 0.99\) A
Step 2: \(G = \dfrac{0.99 \times 0.1}{0.01} = 9.9\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(10.1\ \Omega\) (B) takes the shunt current as \(I + I_g\); the shunt carries only what the galvanometer does not.
Key point: The shunt carries most of the current.

questions.sub_topic: Energy lost when two charged capacitors are joined with opposite polarity
questions.question: Two 2 \(\mu\)F capacitors are each charged to 100 V. The positive plate of each is then joined to the negative plate of the other. The energy lost is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.02 J
Given: \(C = 2\ \mu\text{F}\) each, \(V = 100\) V, so \(Q = 200\ \mu\text{C}\) each
Formula: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\)
Step 1: Initial energy \(= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^4 = 0.02\) J
Step 2: Net charge \(= 200 - 200 = 0\), so the final voltage and energy are zero; all 0.02 J is lost
Common mistake: Zero (B) is the answer for like plates joined: equal voltages, no flow.
Key point: The lost energy goes into heat and radiation in the connecting wires.

questions.sub_topic: Hydrogen spectral series and their regions — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the hydrogen spectrum:
(A) The Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet region.
(B) Some lines of the Balmer series lie in the visible region.
(C) The Paschen series lies in the infrared region.
(D) The Lyman series arises from transitions that end on the \(n = 2\) level.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) jumps to \(n = 1\) release over 10 eV. (B) \(H_\alpha\) at 656 nm is red. (C) jumps to \(n = 3\) release less than 1.6 eV.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Lyman lines end on \(n = 1\); those ending on \(n = 2\) form the Balmer series. Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen end on \(n = 1, 2, 3\).

questions.sub_topic: Energy bands and carriers — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In a metal the valence and conduction bands overlap.
(B) In an n-type semiconductor, holes are the majority carriers.
(C) An insulator has a band gap greater than about 3 eV.
(D) At 0 K a pure semiconductor behaves as an insulator.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: donor atoms in n-type material supply extra electrons, which are the majority carriers.
Why not the others: (A) so electrons move freely. (C) too wide for thermal excitation. (D) no electron has crossed the gap at 0 K. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: n-type means negative (electron) majority carriers.

questions.sub_topic: Energy released when a proton strikes lithium-7
questions.question: In the reaction \(^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \to 2\,{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}\), the atomic masses are \(^{7}\text{Li} = 7.016004\) u, \(^{1}\text{H} = 1.007825\) u and \(^{4}\text{He} = 4.002603\) u. The energy released is about (1 u = 931.5 MeV):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 17.3 MeV
Given: reactants \(8.023829\) u; products \(2 \times 4.002603 = 8.005206\) u
Formula: \(Q = \Delta m \times 931.5\) MeV
Step 1: \(\Delta m = 8.023829 - 8.005206 = 0.018623\) u
Step 2: \(Q = 0.018623 \times 931.5 \approx 17.3\) MeV
Common mistake: 8.7 MeV (B) counts only one helium nucleus. 0.0186 MeV (C) stops at the mass defect in u.
Key point: The mass lost in a reaction appears as kinetic energy of the products.

questions.sub_topic: Power in the 4 Ω branch of a parallel pair with a series resistor
questions.question: Resistors of \(4\ \Omega\) and \(6\ \Omega\) in parallel are joined in series with a \(2.6\ \Omega\) resistor across an ideal 10 V battery. The power used in the \(4\ \Omega\) resistor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5.76 W
Given: \(4 \parallel 6 = \dfrac{24}{10} = 2.4\ \Omega\); total \(= 5\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\), \(P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}\)
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\) A; voltage across the pair \(= 2 \times 2.4 = 4.8\) V
Step 2: \(P_4 = \dfrac{4.8^2}{4} = 5.76\) W
Common mistake: 16 W (A) sends the full 2 A through the \(4\ \Omega\) resistor. 3.84 W (B) is the power in the \(6\ \Omega\) resistor.
Key point: Find the voltage across a parallel group first, then each branch.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Fastest photoelectron from 200 nm light on a 4.2 eV metal
questions.question: Light of wavelength 200 nm falls on a metal of work function 4.2 eV. The maximum speed of the emitted electrons is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm, \(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\) kg):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(8.4 \times 10^{5}\) m s⁻¹
Given: \(\lambda = 200\) nm, \(\phi_0 = 4.2\) eV
Formula: \(K_{max} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\), \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1240}{200} = 6.2\) eV, so \(K_{max} = 2\) eV \(= 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\) J
Step 2: \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.4 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 8.4 \times 10^5\) m s⁻¹
Common mistake: \(1.5 \times 10^6\) (A) uses the whole 6.2 eV. \(7.0 \times 10^{11}\) (D) is \(v^2\).
Key point: Subtract the work function before finding the speed.

questions.sub_topic: Charge on and voltage across the largest of three series capacitors
questions.question: Capacitors of 2 \(\mu\)F, 3 \(\mu\)F and 6 \(\mu\)F are connected in series across a 12 V battery. The charge on the 6 \(\mu\)F capacitor and the voltage across it are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 12 \(\mu\)C and 2 V
Given: \(C_1 = 2\), \(C_2 = 3\), \(C_3 = 6\ \mu\text{F}\); \(V = 12\) V
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dfrac{1}{C_3}\); same \(Q\) on each in series
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = 1\), so \(C = 1\ \mu\text{F}\) and \(Q = 12\ \mu\text{C}\)
Step 2: \(V_3 = \dfrac{Q}{C_3} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\) V
Common mistake: (A) treats the 6 \(\mu\)F capacitor as if it alone were across 12 V. (C) gives the voltage across the 2 \(\mu\)F capacitor.
Key point: In series the largest capacitor takes the smallest voltage.

questions.sub_topic: Force on an electron between plates 2 mm apart at 200 V
questions.question: Two parallel plates 2 mm apart are held at a potential difference of 200 V. The force on an electron between them is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.6 \times 10^{-14}\) N
Given: \(V = 200\) V, \(d = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) m
Formula: \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\), \(F = eE\)
Step 1: \(E = \dfrac{200}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 1 \times 10^5\) V m⁻¹
Step 2: \(F = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^5 = 1.6 \times 10^{-14}\) N, towards the positive plate
Common mistake: \(1.6 \times 10^{-17}\) N (B) takes the 2 mm gap as 2 m.
Key point: The field between parallel plates is uniform, so the force is the same everywhere.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Greatest torque on a 50-turn square coil
questions.question: A square coil of side 4 cm has 50 turns and carries 2 A. The greatest torque on it in a uniform field of 0.5 T is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.08 N m
Given: \(N = 50\), \(A = (0.04)^2 = 1.6 \times 10^{-3}\) m², \(I = 2\) A, \(B = 0.5\) T
Formula: \(\tau_{max} = NIAB\) (field in the plane of the coil)
Step 1: \(\tau = 50 \times 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.5\)
Step 2: \(\tau = 0.08\) N m
Common mistake: 0.8 N m (B) converts 16 cm² to \(1.6 \times 10^{-2}\) m² instead of \(1.6 \times 10^{-3}\).
Key point: The torque is greatest when the field lies in the plane of the coil.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Moving-coil galvanometer and meters — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) An ammeter is made by connecting a high resistance in series with a galvanometer.
(B) The radial field of a moving-coil galvanometer makes its deflection proportional to the current.
(C) Increasing the number of turns of the coil increases the current sensitivity.
(D) An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: an ammeter uses a low resistance (shunt) in parallel; a high series resistance makes a voltmeter.
Why not the others: (B) in a radial field the coil's plane always lies along the field, so the torque is \(NIAB\) at every angle. (C) sensitivity \(= \dfrac{NAB}{k}\). (D) it then draws no current. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Shunt for an ammeter; series resistance for a voltmeter.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Radii of a proton and a deuteron with equal kinetic energy
questions.question: A proton and a deuteron with the same kinetic energy enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles. The ratio of their radii (proton : deuteron) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1 : \sqrt{2}\)
Given: same \(K\), same \(q\); \(m_d = 2m_p\)
Formula: \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(r \propto \sqrt{m}\) at fixed \(K\) and \(q\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{r_p}{r_d} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}} = 1 : \sqrt{2}\)
Common mistake: 1 : 2 (A) is the ratio for equal speeds, where \(r \propto m\).
Key point: Write momentum as \(\sqrt{2mK}\) when kinetic energies are equal.

questions.sub_topic: Virtual image seen through a hollowed glass face
questions.question: An object in air is 30 cm from a concave spherical surface of glass (\(n = 1.5\)) of radius of curvature 20 cm. The image is formed:
options: A) 25.7 cm inside the glass, real
B) 180 cm in front of the surface, virtual
C) 30 cm in front of the surface, virtual
D) 25.7 cm in front of the surface, virtual
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 25.7 cm in front of the surface, virtual
Given: \(n_1 = 1\), \(n_2 = 1.5\), \(u = -30\) cm, \(R = -20\) cm (centre on the object side)
Formula: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1.5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{0.5}{-20} = -\dfrac{1}{40}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1.5}{v} = -\dfrac{7}{120}\), so \(v \approx -25.7\) cm: virtual, on the object side
Common mistake: 180 cm (B) takes \(R\) as positive, as for a convex surface. (A) drops the minus sign of \(v\).
Key point: A concave surface facing the object has its centre on the incident side, so \(R\) is negative.

questions.sub_topic: Wire cut into four equal pieces joined side by side
questions.question: A wire of resistance \(16\ \Omega\) is cut into four equal pieces, which are then joined in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1\ \Omega\)
Given: \(R = 16\ \Omega\), four equal lengths
Formula: \(R \propto l\); \(n\) equal resistors in parallel give \(\dfrac{R}{n}\)
Step 1: Each piece \(= \dfrac{16}{4} = 4\ \Omega\)
Step 2: Four in parallel: \(\dfrac{4}{4} = 1\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(4\ \Omega\) (A) stops at one piece.
Key point: Cutting into \(n\) parts and paralleling them divides the resistance by \(n^2\).

questions.sub_topic: Position and size of the image beyond C for a 15 cm mirror
questions.question: A concave mirror has a focal length of 15 cm. For an object 45 cm away from it, where is the image and how large is it?
options: A) 22.5 cm in front of the mirror, magnification \(-0.5\)
B) 22.5 cm behind the mirror, magnification \(+0.5\)
C) 11.25 cm in front of the mirror, magnification \(-0.25\)
D) 45 cm in front of the mirror, magnification \(-1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 22.5 cm in front of the mirror, magnification \(-0.5\)
Given: \(u = -45\) cm, \(f = -15\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}\), \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{45} = -\dfrac{2}{45}\), so \(v = -22.5\) cm
Step 2: \(m = -\dfrac{-22.5}{-45} = -0.5\): real, inverted, half size
Common mistake: 11.25 cm (C) adds \(\dfrac{1}{15}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{45}\), losing the sign of \(u\).
Key point: An object beyond \(2f\) gives a real, smaller image between \(f\) and \(2f\).

questions.sub_topic: Relaxed-eye magnification of a 5 cm magnifying glass
questions.question: A magnifying glass of focal length 5 cm is adjusted so that the final image is at infinity (\(D = 25\) cm). The angular magnification it gives is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5
Given: \(f = 5\) cm, \(D = 25\) cm
Formula: \(m = \dfrac{D}{f}\) (image at infinity)
Step 1: \(m = \dfrac{25}{5} = 5\)
Common mistake: 6 (A) is the value with the image at the near point, \(1 + \dfrac{D}{f}\).
Key point: Viewing at infinity costs one unit of magnification but rests the eye.

questions.sub_topic: Force between two identical spheres after they touch
questions.question: Two identical small conducting spheres carry \(+6\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(-2\ \mu\text{C}\) and attract each other with a force \(F\). They are made to touch and then returned to the same separation. The force between them is now:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{F}{3}\), repulsive
Given: \(q_1 = +6\ \mu\text{C}\), \(q_2 = -2\ \mu\text{C}\); identical spheres share charge equally
Formula: \(F = \dfrac{k|q_1q_2|}{r^2}\)
Step 1: After contact each has \(\dfrac{6 - 2}{2} = +2\ \mu\text{C}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{F'}{F} = \dfrac{2 \times 2}{6 \times 2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\); like charges, so repulsive
Common mistake: (A) gets the size but keeps the old direction; both spheres are now positive.
Key point: Contact shares the net charge, which can flip attraction into repulsion.

questions.sub_topic: Diverging lens with the object at its focal distance
questions.question: A diverging lens of focal length 12 cm has an object at a distance equal to its focal length. The image is formed:
options: A) 6 cm on the other side of the lens, real
B) 6 cm on the same side as the object, virtual and half size
D) 12 cm on the same side as the object, same size
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6 cm on the same side as the object, virtual and half size
Given: \(u = -12\) cm, \(f = -12\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\), \(m = \dfrac{v}{u}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{12} = -\dfrac{1}{6}\), so \(v = -6\) cm
Step 2: \(m = \dfrac{-6}{-12} = 0.5\): virtual, erect, half size
Common mistake: (C) treats it like a convex lens with the object at its focus.
Key point: A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, smaller image.

questions.sub_topic: Work and energy in four electrostatic processes
questions.question:
Match each process in List-I with the work done or energy involved in List-II.

List-I
(A) Moving a 5 \(\mu\)C charge along an equipotential surface
(B) Taking a 2 \(\mu\)C charge from a point at 0 V to a point at 100 V
(C) Bringing two 1 \(\mu\)C charges from infinity to 1 m apart
(D) Charging a 1 \(\mu\)F capacitor to 100 V (energy stored)

List-II
(I) \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) J
(II) zero
(III) \(9 \times 10^{-3}\) J
(IV) \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) J
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Along an equipotential \(\Delta V = 0\), so \(W = 0\) (II)
Step 2: \(W = q\Delta V = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\) J (IV)
Step 3: \(U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-12} = 9 \times 10^{-3}\) J (III)
Step 4: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-6} \times 10^4 = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) J (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (C) and (D); the pair of charges needs \(\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}\), the capacitor \(\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\).
Key point: Work depends only on the potential difference between the end points.

questions.sub_topic: Mobility from drift speed and field
questions.question: Electrons in a conductor drift at \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) m s⁻¹ in an electric field of 0.5 V m⁻¹. Their mobility is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(5 \times 10^{-4}\) m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹
Given: \(v_d = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) m s⁻¹, \(E = 0.5\) V m⁻¹
Formula: \(\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E}\)
Step 1: \(\mu = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-4}}{0.5} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹
Common mistake: (A) multiplies by \(E\). (C) inverts the ratio.
Key point: Mobility is drift speed per unit field.
